result:
There's a particular quality to the light in a kitchen at 6:47 in the morning that I've never seen anywhere else, in anyone else's kitchen, at any other time. It comes through a window that's been slightly fogged from last night's shower, and it hits the linoleum at a low angle, long and thin, the way morning light always does when it's still too cold for the sun to climb properly. And in that light, you can see the dust moving. Not settling. *Moving*. Suspended in the shaft like the memory of something that used to be real.

I think about this more than I'd like to admit. Not in some grand, philosophical way, but in the small way that a person standing by the counter with a mug of coffee that's gone too cool thinks about a specific Tuesday in 2014 when they forgot their keys and called a locksmith at 7:15 and the man who came had a ring of blue paint on his left index finger and said, in a voice that had the texture of a television left on in another room, "These are going to be tough." And then he was done, the lock clicked, and he left, and I never found out his name, and I don't even remember the week or the month. But the blue paint is there, vivid as a thumbnail sketch, and it means something to me. It means *that was the world, and I was in it, and the lock opened, and the day continued.*

This is what I find strange about time, if I'm honest. People talk about it as if it's a river, a line, a thing that moves. But experience suggests it's more like a room. You're in the kitchen. The light is at this angle. The coffee is cold. You think of 2014 and the locksmith's finger and it's as immediate as the dust in the shaft of light. It's not *behind* you. It's *in* the same room. You've always been in the same room. You just move your gaze.

And this gets weird in a specific way. I was in a hardware store last month, the kind on the edge of a small town, the kind where the owner knows your name because everyone does. I picked up a pair of needle-nose pliers. Just pliers. And I held them, and I thought about how the man who made them was sitting at a bench. How the steel was heated and bent and cooled. How the handles were made from some alloy chosen because it felt right in the palm of a hand, and that "right" is not a measurement but a conversation between the metal and the nerve ending in your thumb. And the whole chain of choices and hands and purposes extended back to a mine in a country I couldn't name, and forward to a person who will hold these pliers to fix a leaky pipe in a house that doesn't exist yet, in a decade I won't live to see. I was holding a sentence that was still being written.

I set the pliers back down. The owner said something about the new price on the pliers. I bought them. I don't know why. They'll probably sit in a drawer for three years. They'll acquire a thin film of grime and a smell like old gasoline and the specific mustiness of a drawer that isn't opened. And one day I'll need them, or I won't. If I won't, they'll be a small fossil of a Tuesday in a hardware store, and the blue paint will be somewhere else, on some other finger, in some other moment I'll forget the name of the person who wore it.

But I want to say something about the morning light specifically. Because I think the light is honest in a way that other things aren't. It doesn't care about your mortgage or your argument with your sibling or whether you've been sleeping too well lately. It just hits the floor at an angle. It does its thing. The dust moves because the light makes the dust visible, or maybe because the warm air from the hot water tap is doing something invisible and the light is just giving it a place to show up. Either way, the dust moves, and you watch it for eleven seconds, and those eleven seconds are yours and no one's ever watched that particular movement before.

I think we spend most of our lives avoiding that. We scroll. We narrate. We explain. We put words over the moment so we don't have to just *watch the dust move.* We build a story around the Tuesday, around the locksmith, around the pliers, because a story is more secure. A story has a beginning and an end. A moment in a kitchen at 6:47 doesn't. It just is. And the not-having-an-end is the thing that frightens us, or maybe just the thing that's quiet.

I made coffee. It's hot now. The light is at a different angle because it's 7:02 and the sun has climbed. The dust is in the other shaft of light, or maybe there's only one shaft now and I'm just not seeing it. I pour the coffee. I drink it. I think about blue paint on a finger that doesn't belong to me. I think about the man in the mine. I think about the woman who'll fix the pipe in the house that doesn't exist yet.

The coffee is almost cool. The light is moving. The dust doesn't stop.
